name: Crossplane
summary: Turns a Kubernetes cluster into a control plane for infrastructure: you declare a bucket or a database as a Kubernetes object, and controllers create it and keep putting it back if it drifts.
intro: Crossplane runs as controllers in a Kubernetes cluster. A provider, installed as a package, adds managed resources: ready-made custom resources such as an S3 `Bucket` or an RDS `Instance`. Each has a controller that calls the cloud’s API to make the real resource match the object’s spec, using credentials named in a ProviderConfig. It doesn’t stop after creating it: the controller polls the resource, and if someone changes it in the console, the next reconcile corrects the drift. The poll interval can be set per resource with an annotation.

Composition is how a platform team publishes its own APIs. A CompositeResourceDefinition declares a new kind, such as `App` or `Database`, and a Composition runs a pipeline of functions, written in YAML, KCL, Python or Go, that returns the resources to create for it. Crossplane 2.0 (August 2025) made composite and managed resources namespaced by default, let a composition include any Kubernetes resource such as a Deployment next to an RDS instance, dropped the separate claim objects, and added Operations for one-off, scheduled or event-driven jobs. Crossplane is a CNCF graduated project.
strengths: Continuous reconciliation: drift is corrected on the next poll rather than the next time someone runs an apply, and stable resources can be polled less often
Platform teams offer their own APIs (an `App`, a `Database`) without writing a controller, and users reach them with kubectl, Kubernetes RBAC and namespaces
Fits the Kubernetes toolchain: Argo CD or Flux sync it from git, and it works with Helm, Kyverno, Open Policy Agent, Prometheus and Backstage
Vendor-neutral under the CNCF and Apache 2.0, including the AWS, Azure and GCP providers Upbound donated in 2023
limits: Needs a Kubernetes cluster (the getting-started guide asks for at least 2 GB of RAM), and that cluster becomes critical infrastructure
Big providers add many CRDs: provider-aws-ec2 alone installs about 200, at roughly 3 MiB of API server memory each, unless you activate only the ones you use
Operations, managed resource definitions and activation policies are still alpha features in v2
Hard to learn: in 2023 the project itself called the path to a production-ready control plane difficult, and debugging means following objects and events across Crossplane, provider and function pods

story: By 2018 Kubernetes had become the standard way to run containers portably, but most workloads also leaned on managed databases, queues and buckets, each behind its cloud’s proprietary API. Running those services on Kubernetes yourself with operators brought the operating burden back. Upbound’s founders argued for “a new portability layer on top of existing managed services”: a control plane with one declarative API across providers.

Bassam Tabbara, Illya Chekrygin and Jared Watts introduced Crossplane on December 4, 2018 as an “open source multicloud control plane”. It reused the unmodified Kubernetes API server and etcd, and the first design had resource claims and classes, so developers asked for a database and administrators decided how it was provisioned, plus a scheduler meant to place workloads across clouds. It joined the CNCF as a sandbox project in 2020 and moved to incubating in 2021.

Over time the focus moved from multicloud portability to platform engineering. In September 2023 Upbound donated its Upjet framework and its AWS, Azure and GCP providers to the project, which widened its charter to providers and developer tooling. Crossplane 2.0 (August 12, 2025) dropped claims and cluster-scoped defaults, saying v1 “had become overly opinionated”, and on November 6, 2025 the CNCF announced its graduation, counting more than 3,000 contributors from over 450 organizations and over 100 releases.

choices.choice: Build on the Kubernetes API server instead of a new one
choices.why: The team expected the model to feel familiar to the cloud native community and to reuse its tools, UIs and language bindings, so it could focus on multicloud problems “instead of reinventing machinery”.

choices.choice: Reconcile continuously instead of plan and apply
choices.why: A control plane configures software and then watches it for its whole life, so drift from the desired state is corrected automatically without involving an admin.

choices.choice: Composition as a pipeline of functions
choices.why: Writing a Kubernetes controller for every custom API is hard to get right; functions return declarative configuration and let teams express the logic in YAML, KCL, Python or Go.

choices.choice: Namespaced resources by default in v2
choices.why: Claims and cluster-scoped resources had “created unnecessary friction”; namespaces match Kubernetes conventions and make multi-tenancy simpler.
